extracted.intended_audience: mathematical-olympiad contestants, problem solvers, and advanced undergraduate readers studying olympiad-style solutions
extracted.subtask_description: Solutions and worked lemmas for several olympiad-style problems (inequalities, number theory, trigonometry, geometry, and polynomial congruences). The page presents definitions, lemmas, multiple solution methods, and remarks about equality/counterexample cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Majorization (definition and Birkhoff representation)
rubrics_metrics.description: If u = (u1,...,un) and v = (v1,...,vn) are two nonincreasing sequences, u majorizes v if u1+...+ui >= v1+...+vi for i = 1,...,n and u1+...+un = v1+...+vn. By Birkhoff's theorem there exist constants c_σ in [0,1] with Σ_{σ∈S} c_σ = 1 and Σ_{σ∈S} c_σ a_{σ(i)} = b_i for i = 1,...,n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to reduce comparisons between sequences to convex combinations of permutations; the representation provides a way to average permutation-based expressions and deduce inequalities. The page uses this to prove an inequality and to obtain equality conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove inequality and check equality case
rubrics_metrics.description: We will prove the inequality Σ_{i,j=1}^n |a_i - a_j| ≥ Σ_{i,j=1}^n |b_i - b_j| with equality if and only if a_i = b_i for i = 1,...,n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When proving such inequalities, explicitly state and verify the equality condition; track when all intermediate inequalities are equalities to deduce necessary equality conditions on variables (here, the sequences). The solution shows how to carry equality through a convex-combination argument and a lemma.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permutation inversion lemma
rubrics_metrics.description: Lemma: Let σ be a permutation of {1,...,n} and let (a1,...,an) be real numbers. If (a_{σ(1)},...,a_{σ(n)}) = (a1,...,an) and there exist indices i,j with a_i < a_j but a_{σ(i)} > a_{σ(j)}, then there exist i,j with the stated property (proof by induction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This structural lemma is used to conclude that if signs of certain differences must be the same for all σ in S, then the underlying sequence must be unchanged by the permutations in S. It is introduced as a technical combinatorial tool to finish equality-case arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of Chebyshev-type monic polynomials Sn
rubrics_metrics.description: For every positive integer n there is a monic polynomial S_n(x) with integer coefficients such that S_n(2 cos α) = 2 cos(nα).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This fact (proved by induction using addition-to-product formulas) is used in trigonometric-number-theory problems to relate rationality of cosines at rational-multiple angles to algebraic integer properties; it motivates argument via integer polynomials and Gauss' lemma.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rational cosine values for rational multiple of π (lemma)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lemma: If cos α is rational and α = rπ for some rational r, then the possible values of cos α are 0, ±1/2, ±1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses the Sn(x) polynomial and Gauss' lemma to deduce that 2 cos α is an integer; since |2 cos α| ≤ 2 the only integer possibilities are 0, ±1, ±2, yielding the listed cosine values. Use this when combining rationality information with angle rationality to restrict possible angles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationality propagation for cosine: if cos x rational then cos(nx) rational
rubrics_metrics.description: If cos x is rational then cos(n x) is rational for every positive integer n (follows from the recurrence/product-to-sum relations or by applying Sn).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This property is used to propagate rationality assumptions and obtain contradictions with irrationality assumptions; it simplifies arguments by reducing to a rational-algebraic setting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Periodic divisibility lemma for powers: bn+φ(a) ≡ bn (mod a) for large n
rubrics_metrics.description: Lemma: Given positive integers a and b, for sufficiently large n we have b^{n+φ(a)} ≡ b^n (mod a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use prime factorization of a, multiplicativity of φ, and Euler's theorem to show eventual periodicity of b^n modulo each prime power dividing a, then combine via Chinese Remainder Theorem. This supports constructions and inductive arguments about divisibility properties of power sequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inductive reduction strategy for divisibility properties
rubrics_metrics.description: To show statements about divisibility of b^n by a for infinitely many n, reduce a by removing prime divisors step-by-step (either by reducing to φ(a) < a through induction or removing largest prime factors one by one), using periodicity modulo prime powers and CRT to combine congruences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two alternative reduction strategies are presented: reduce modulus size via φ(a) (faster conceptual reduction), or remove prime divisors one-by-one starting from the largest prime (constructive CRT-based progression). Choose method suited to quantitative or structural needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: reduced polynomial for remainder-sequence classification
rubrics_metrics.description: A polynomial P(x) = a0 + a1 x + ... + a5 x^5 with integer coefficients is called reduced if for i = 0,...,5 we have 0 ≤ a_i < b_i (with specified b_i on the page).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any polynomial's remainder sequence modulo 1024 at odd arguments can be matched by a reduced polynomial by repeatedly subtracting suitable integer multiples of specially chosen polynomials Q_i(x) (each Q_i(x) divisible by 2^k for odd x). This gives a finite canonical set to enumerate possible remainder sequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction rule: subtract multiples of Qi(x) without changing remainder sequence
rubrics_metrics.description: For i = 0,...,6 and any integer-coefficient polynomial R(x), P(x) and P(x) - R(x)Q_i(x) have the same remainder sequence because Q_i(x) is divisible by 2^{?} (in the text, by 2^{something}/210) for any odd integer x.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides the algorithmic step for reducing an arbitrary polynomial to a reduced representative (lower-degree or with coefficients in canonical ranges) while preserving the remainder sequence on odd inputs modulo 1024; iterate from highest-degree terms downward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parity criteria for complete remainder sequences (completeness constraints)
rubrics_metrics.description: A remainder sequence (r(1),r(3),...,r(1023)) is a permutation of (1,3,...,1023) (i.e., complete) only if the reduced polynomial satisfies specific parity conditions: a1 + a3 + a5 is odd (so polynomial yields odd remainders) and a0 + a1 + a2 + a3 + a4 + a5 is odd (overall parity constraint described on the page).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page pairs reduced polynomials to count those satisfying parity constraints and thereby bounds the number of different complete remainder sequences (concluding a limit like 2^something or 235 in the text). Use pairing arguments (P(x) with P(x)+x or P(x)+1) to enumerate parity classes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symmedian lemma in cyclic/tangent geometry: AT is a symmedian
rubrics_metrics.description: Lemma: In triangle ABC inscribed in circle ω, with BT and CT tangent at B and C respectively and M the midpoint of BC, we have ∠BAT = ∠CAM (line AT is a symmedian).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use similarity of triangles formed by tangents and chords, equal tangents TB = TC, and Ptolemy's theorem to deduce ratios leading to the symmedian property. This lemma is used to relate angles and apply the Law of Sines to obtain similarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete-residue condition for integer sequence problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Condition: For sequence (a_i), for every positive integer n, the numbers a1,...,an leave distinct remainders modulo n (equivalently, form a complete set of residues modulo n).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This condition is the hypothesis of an IMO-style problem; use it to deduce (1) all terms are distinct, (2) bounds on distances between terms, (3) existence of blocks of consecutive integers among first n terms, and finally (4) that every integer appears exactly once in the sequence. The page outlines the four-step argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of classical inequalities and symmetric-sum techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: Techniques used repeatedly: Cauchy–Schwarz, AM–GM, Weighted AM–GM, symmetric sums/symmetrization, and manipulations with homogeneous inequalities (normalization like xyz=1 or x^2+y^2+z^2 fixed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When proving homogeneous inequalities reduce by scaling (e.g., assume xyz=1 or set a symmetric normalization), then apply known inequalities and/or form symmetric sums and compare term-by-term using AM–GM with suitable weights. The page exhibits multiple solutions following these patterns and emphasizes verifying equality or extremal cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check necessity of hypotheses and construct counterexamples when dropped
rubrics_metrics.description: Remarks: "Note also that it is an easy exercise with generating functions to construct counterexamples if you drop the majorization condition..." and other notes indicating the importance of retaining hypotheses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always assess whether stated conditions (like majorization or irrationality) are necessary; try to construct counterexamples when a hypothesis is removed to test sharpness. The page uses such notes to explain why certain constraints cannot be omitted.
